paragraphs.text: Welcome to Behind the Ticker, the podcast where we go beyond the symbol and into the strategy. I'm Brad Roth, founder and chief investment officer at Thor Funds. And in each episode, I sit down with ETF managers, CIOs, and industry leaders to break down how these funds are actually built, how they behave in real markets, and how advisors use them in real portfolios. Most people just see a ticker symbol, but we know much more goes on behind the ticker. Hey, Mike, welcome to the show.

Thanks, Brad. Thanks for having me. So why don't you take some time, give everybody a bit about your background. I saw you went to Boston College for Economics and Finance. You were at FTI Consulting for a little bit. I've got a couple of buddies that are actually still there. And you joined Hilton Capital in 2024. We're now co-portfolio manager on HBDC. Can you kind of just walk us through your career path and how it all unfolded? Yeah, yeah, absolutely. Yeah. So I've been in the business now since 2018. So like you mentioned, I graduated Boston College, econ and finance degrees. Started my career at FTI in restructuring. So it was a consulting job, but it was a little bit more niche in the sense that it was

Looking at companies that were going through the Chapter 11 restructuring process. So they were going through some sort of significant distress event for them. So we would come in there primarily on the debtor side, work out the cash flow liquidity analysis that was needed to get this business to get Chapter 11 protection and work out some sort of deal with their creditors. So I did that for two years, really got in the weeds on detailed modeling and so forth. And I loved it. It was a great experience. But what I realized there was, hey, you know what? I love the strategy component, not so much the deep implementation. And investing is much more focused on strategy and higher level thinking and less on let's go down to an accounting ledger and

Look at APAR analysis really, really deeply. So after two years of doing restructuring, I said, you know what? I want to go on the investing side of finance instead of the restructuring side. So that actually led me to become a sell-side equity analyst, which is kind of ironic because now we're running a bond fund. But I was an equity analyst at a company called Wolf Research, which is, I believe, the fifth or sixth largest sell-side equity research shop in the U.S. So I worked under an institutional investor-ranked analyst called Chris Sennick. He ran the macro and accounting and special sits product over at Wolf. But there, I was his VP. So I was working primarily on the special sit side, special situation side of his book. So looking at

Niche-y spinoffs, restructurings, asset sales, stuff that was kind of underlooked by the market, underfollowed, and so forth. So we would do the detailed modeling and so forth, put a valuation target on that, and publish research to our clients, which were primarily long-only asset managers and hedge funds. And I did that for about three and a half years, really got in the weeds on looking at valuations, looking at cash flow analysis, and so forth, and loved it there. But as I got into my late 20s, now in my 30s, I said, you know what, now is the time to really put your money where your mouth is, and let's take a crack on the buy side. So that's when I joined Hilton Capital Management in 2024. And we are now about a $4 billion asset manager. When I joined,

It was about $2 billion. So we've really grown pretty substantially over the last two and a half years here. And originally, we had three products. It was a multi-asset tactical income strategy, which I'll get into a little bit, and that's actually how HBDC became where it is now. A long-only equity dividend and yield strategy, and then a small-cap strategy as well. So we run those three strategies. I personally run with our CIO, Alex Oxingham, the tactical income strategy, the dividend yield strategy, and then now HBDC as well. We launched last year in June of 2025, a new passive ETF called HBDC, the Hilton Capital BDC Bond Fund, which is a little ironic because we're an active manager launching a passive ETF. But there was a lot of thought process going into the index,

And it being the first and only pure play BDC bond ETF out there. We just wanted to offer a solution to get investors to have a nice liquid alternative to get access in that space. So happy to go kind of how that came in to be. But yeah, now we're at Hilton, about $4 billion with four strategies now. Yeah, we're going to go pretty deep on HBDC here in a second. Before we do that, though, I always like to ask people, when you're not working, what do you like to do? Any hobbies outside of work? Yeah, so I do like to play golf quite a bit, which, here at Hilton, it's kind of our flagship hobby. I also recently bought a house about a year and a half ago.

So I'm really into home renovation and DIY projects these days. Yeah, well, I have gone through the DIY phase of my life. Just make sure you're outsourcing the stuff that will get you hurt. Yeah, exactly. So let's get into HBDC. So it's the Hilton BDC corporate bond ETF. Like you said, you launched it in June of 2025. At a high level, what is this fund? And what's the problem that it's solving? Yeah, so like I mentioned, it's the first and only pure play BDC bond ETF out there. So BDC is to just take a step back. It stands for business development companies. They've been around for quite a while. They've actually been around since 1980 as an amendment to the Investment Company Act of 1940. And what their purpose was and still is, is to lend to medium and small businesses,

Primarily in the US. So think of them like banks without actually the deposits. So how they get their capital to lend out is primarily three ways. They issue bonds to the public market, they issue equity, and then they also sometimes have a direct line of credit as well. And then they lend these loans out to small and medium-sized companies, primarily floating rate loans, which is now their asset side. And they make money off the spread of what they borrow on and what they can lend on. They were always kind of a small part of the market historically. But after the great financial crisis of 08-09 and banking regulation really stepped up quite a bit, BDCs filled a lot of the void that was left after the crisis in 2009. So BDC assets have grown pretty substantially over the last 15

Or so years. And many folks know BDCs on the equity side. BizD, for example, is a very large ETF that tracks BDC equity. But there was nothing out there that tracked the BDC bonds themselves. So these are bonds that are directly issued by the BDCs themselves that are used to finance the loans that they make in these small and medium-sized companies. What kind of attracted us to the space is, like I mentioned at Hilton, we've been running our tactical income strategy, which is about $2.5 billion of assets for over 25 years now, and have owned several of these bonds in the past. They're pretty short-duration bonds, typically three to five years duration. And they have pretty juicy spreads on them.

They're typically about 200 to 300 basis points over like-duration Treasuries, 100 to 200 basis points over like-duration IG Corporates. And these bonds are overwhelmingly investment-grade. So we've owned them for quite a while. And running the strategies, we said, hey, you know what? There's no ETF that actually tracks these bonds out there. And a lot of advisors and clients that we were talking to, yeah, they would own the big bonds like the Aries and the Golubs out there. But some of the smaller ones out there, they would have no exposure to them. So we said, hey, you know what? Let's wrap this up in an ETF. Let's make a really detail-oriented index. There was no index out there. And then let's track it and launch this ETF. So now HBDC is the first and only pure play bond BDC ETF out there.

And when we constructed the index, we partnered with a German company called Selective. They're pretty large. They do a lot of indexes out there. And given that most of these BDC bonds are overwhelmingly the very large guys, as you can imagine, like the Aries, the Blue Owls of the world out there, we didn't want it to be overly concentrated in those BDCs themselves. So we actually capped the top two largest issuers at 10%. And then the second largest issuer is at eight. And then the following two at seven. And then everybody else is capped at five. So the index itself and the ETF by and large actually overweights the smaller BDCs by design to get you a little extra spread in the index. And so currently right now, HBDC, it pays about a yield to maturity of about 6.7%.

It's almost 95% investment grade bonds. And the spread on that is about, I think, 175 basis points over like duration treasuries. So it's pretty attractive yield and spread, especially for an overwhelmingly investment grade portfolio. So I see, we've been seeing in the news a lot about private credit. It's been one of the biggest stories in finance over the last few years. How does owning BDC bonds, given investors never heard of a BDC bond, like access in a way to that market? Yeah. So I like to say it's tangent to the private credit market. This ETF does not own the direct loans that these BDCs are making to these small and medium sized companies. It's the bonds that they're issuing to get the capital so they can then lend out to these small and medium sized

Companies. But that actually has some structural protections in place and why we like these bonds. So BDCs, by law, actually can only leverage up their balance sheets a max two to one. So what that means is for every $2 of debt, they have to have a dollar of equity cushion below it. That's in comparison to banks that are levered at eight to one or even larger than that. So when you buy a bank bond, you're essentially buying a balance sheet that's levered eight to one and no one really bats an high on some of these large cap banks. So there's substantially more equity cushion on these BDCs. And most BDCs, including the large ones, like I mentioned, Aries and so forth, run their balance sheets significantly more conservatively than their max statutory leverage ratios. Most of them are one

To one or even less than one to one. So there's a lot of cushion in place. So just to kind of conceptualize that, if you run your balance sheet at a max two to one ratio, you would need a 50% drawdown on the NAV before the bonds would start to be impaired, which is a pretty substantial credit event and has actually never happened throughout the history of BDCs existing. And going back all the way to 1980, there has never been a BDC bond impairment. So there's been many credit cycles since 1980, and these bonds have held up quite well. So you talked a little bit about the index design in partnership with Selectives. Can you walk us through the rules a little bit deeper? So you've got

Investment grade, fixed rate, senior unsecured, and then there's a $250 million minimum issue size. Like why those screens? Just talk us through the construction again. Yeah, yeah, absolutely. Just to clarify, so there actually is no investment grade mandate. So these bonds can go to junk bonds, and we would still own them. Just over the space overwhelmingly right now is investment grade. And the reason why we did that is because if we went through a credit event, I would suspect that some of these bonds would be downgraded. But due to the structural protections that we talked about, we wouldn't want to not own these in the index. And we wanted to give investors a broad space of the BDC bonds themselves. So we didn't want to just isolate it to just investment

Grade. So right now, it's 95 plus percent investment grade, but it could go down a little bit if there ever is a significant credit event. But of the index criteria that we designed, like I mentioned, we have those structural percentage caps on there to provide diversification benefits. The minimum issuance size of $250 million was in place, mostly because we didn't really want to have any sort of illiquidity events that could really impair some of our investors. When bond issuance are smaller than $250 million issuance sizes, it typically gets hard to buy them. And given that we're rebalancing this index quarterly, we're obviously turning over the index four times a year. And sometimes, like we did see earlier in this year, there could be some illiquid pockets in the

Market. But that is overwhelmingly in the smaller issuances. So we put that cap limit of $250 and over to protect investors from that. And we did a liquidity stress test when we were putting the ETF together with the regulators. And to buy the least liquid bond in the portfolio, you would need about a daily inflow-outflow of about $400 million. So that's a pretty substantial inflow-outflow of the ETF, which we don't even have those assets in the ETF at the moment. Hopefully we will soon. But that's meaning that it's pretty liquid. And we're pretty happy with the construction of it. So I've talked to a lot of advisors over the last 10 years. I've never heard someone talk to me about BDC bond exposure. So let's bring this back to very simple terms. Where do BDC bonds sit on the yield

And risk spectrum compared to what they're more traditionally used to hold, like investment-grade corporates or high yields or the ag? Yeah, yeah. So if you look at a cap structure of a BDC, or really any company, because the BDC is just a company at the end of the day, you have equity, which is right at the bottom of the Tron structure. So those guys, when you're owning BizD and ARCC equity, yes, they have very large dividends, but you're at the very bottom of the capital structure. Meaning if there's ever sort of an impairment to NAV and so forth, you're the first ones that are taking the losses. Then on top of the equity, you sometimes have preferred equity or convertible preferreds as well. Typically, if you have a significant event, obviously like a Chapter 11 type of process,

Those would get wiped out as well. And then on top of that, that's where BDC bonds sit, is the senior unsecured bonds. And then within bonds themselves, sometimes you have senior unsecured and you have junior and so forth. All these bonds in our portfolio are senior unsecured. So they're on the very, very top of the bond structure, meaning that they sit pretty high up there. There are, however, sometimes not BDCs, but some companies do secured bonds, meaning that they're tied directly to some sort of asset on their balance sheet. So those would sit above that. And then if there's any sort of secured direct lending or so forth, line of credit, that would sit at the very, very top. So when you look at a cap structure, I would say BDC bonds in

HBDC sit towards the middle or higher portion of the capital structure. So there's a lot of cushion below these bonds. So, like we mentioned, you would need a significant credit event to even get, be worried about these bonds. And that's kind of the opportunity here because the spreads and the yields maturities on these bonds are, we think, discriminately high for a security that has a lot of structural protections in place. So liquidity is always a question in a niche bond market. So how does the ETF wrapper help that? And how does the index handle liquidity at the security level? Yeah. So, well, when, within any ETF and with our ETF as well, you have creation and redemption units.

So what that is, is we have a lead market maker that would buy these securities or they could do an income or in cash creation redemption. And so they're the ones that are actually trading it and putting it together. So what that does is even if there is, let's say a million dollars in the ETF, which be relatively small, which there is not, but in the case of this example, there could be, and someone wants to put a $10 million, buy order in the ETF, that would not impact the trading dynamics of the ETF. The lead market maker would then buy all the bonds in the portfolio and then structure that at the $10 million, ticket price. So I think a lot of advisors mistakenly see an ETF

That may only have a few assets in it, or, maybe 10 million of assets in it and say, oh, it's illiquid. If I put a big ticket order in it, it's going to, be hard to buy or sell that ETF. It's not actually true. It's, it's the underlying assets in the ETF that matter more so than the ETF itself. And given that B the BDC bond market is now a $70 billion plus market, it's a very, very liquid market. I wouldn't say, well, I should say it's liquid enough, not extremely liquid, but it's liquid enough that any sizable ticket order, like I mentioned, under 400 million daily should have no problem buying or selling, HBDC. So you guys just actually crossed a hundred million in assets about seven months after launch.

What's been driving that demand from advisors? What have you learned so far? this is a very niche new market. You're the only player in the space today. So what's it like? What have you learned? Yeah. So there's definitely a bit of a learning curve. So when we meet with advisors and they say, okay, yeah, this looks really cool, but why don't I just own biz D? It has a higher yield. And then we have to explain, what, what the tron structure is and, what equity versus debt is and so forth. And I would say, 85 to 90% of advisors that once we explain it to them, they then get it pretty quickly. Um, and they say, oh, this is pretty attractive to me.

Um, and so forth. Um, so that was definitely, we expected it, but we didn't expect it to be as thorough as, as, as it turned out to be that almost every single call we meet with advisor group was, okay, explain to me the difference between HBDC and biz D out there. Why are you paying a lower yield than biz D and so forth? Um, that was the one thing, but like I mentioned, we kind of give that 10 minute, 10, 15 minute, educational, uh, lesson, and then they usually get it pretty quickly. Um, then the second thing is, as you probably are well aware of this year has been, uh, there's no shortage of negative press in the private credit world out there.

Um, there's a lot of, fear taglines out there and so forth. Um, we could talk a little bit about that and why I think it's, it's overblown. Um, and that's the second part of the conversations that we're having is, Hey, I hear a private, private credit's going to blow up any day now. Nobody knows, what's going on there and so forth. Um, and kind of going back to the educational, uh, lessons that we tell advisors is BDCs are actually remarkably transparent. Uh, so even private BDCs, which some of them issue public bonds that are in HBC, every single one of them has to publish a 10 K, uh, report with the SEC and file that.

And in the 10 K, they put every single loan, classify it by the sector and so forth, the terms and all that stuff, uh, out there. So you can actually dig down into each and every, uh, BDC and see where they're lending money to and what the terms are and so forth. Um, so they're remarkably transparent, even though the press seems to love to say that they're not, but they, they really are. Um, so that has been a hurdle, uh, for sure is just kind of fighting the tide of the negative press cycle out there. Um, and don't get me wrong. There are some, yellow flags and some red flags out there in the private credit world, um, that we could talk about for sure. Uh, but within the BDC

Space at large, again, these are smaller loans themselves to small and medium sized U S focus companies. Um, we're actually starting to see non-accruals and pick income and so forth, uh, stabilize and actually take down. Um, so I think that is helped us a little bit recently. Um, and then there's also, the kind of expansion that was in the late early 2020s and so forth of selling these private BDCs to a lot of advisors and so forth. And then they didn't read the five print to, uh, to, uh, too closely. And they say, Hey, I can only redeem my assets at 5% a quarter, I want all my money back now. Um, which, that's a fair criticism. Um, but that has actually been a tailwind for HBDC because given that it is an ETF,

There is no lockups, there is no, uh, illiquidity events, uh, you can buy and sell it the same day if you really wanted to. Um, so that's been a bit of a tailwind for, for, for our ETF. So for an advisor, like thinking about HBDC, how would they use it in a client's fixed income allocation? Is this like a core compliment? Is it an income sleeve? Like how do you educate on how it should be utilized? I wouldn't be out here and say it's a substitute for the ag, your core bond fund, uh, because this is a more niche part of the market and BDC bonds do gap out on their spreads when you get some sort of, uh, financial stress in the system. Um, I think

That's a great buying opportunity because they always snap right back. Um, but they will be a little bit more volatile than your, traditional investment grade bonds. And we've run the analysis on that, uh, going back over the last, uh, uh, five plus years, the beta on these bonds is about 1.4, meaning that if spreads blow out about a hundred basis points for investment grade bonds, we would expect BDC bonds to blow out about 140 basis points. So they're not a direct substitute for your core bond fund. Uh, what I think they are, uh, a good substitute is, is if you have any allocation towards alternatives out there and you're in some of these interval funds and you're in some of these private BDC funds out there, uh, and you're getting frustrated saying, Hey, there's lockups

In place. They're not really performing that well. The fees are incredibly high. Some of them are 2% management fees and so forth. Uh, I think this is a great substitute for that because this is liquid. It's traded daily. It's, it's relatively cheap. It's only 39 basis points. Um, and you're getting that exposure, uh, to the alternative asset management space, uh, via BDC bonds. Uh, so that's where we're seeing a lot of traction, uh, there we're also seeing, some traction with some insurance companies as well. Uh, we are, uh, NAIC, uh, 2C rated. Uh, we just got that. Um, so some insurance companies have really started to embrace, uh, HBDC as well. Well, Mike, I really appreciate you spending some time with me today before I can let you go.

Where can people learn more about Hilton Capital and HBDC? Yeah, sure. So, uh, if you go to our website, which is, uh, HiltonCapitalManagement.com, uh, you can go and see our strategies, all of them and select HBDC. And there's tons of fact sheets and marketing material out there, uh, for anyone that's interested. Well, again, Mike, thanks for hanging out. Yeah. Thanks for having me. Appreciate it.
